# Type Conversion Operators
<!-- Slide 11 -->

## Teach Temperature to Become a double {.smaller}

- `Temperature today(21.5);`
- `double reading = today;` needs a rule the compiler does not have.

::: notes
Slides 12–18

Pick up directly from the error at the end of the review.
:::

<!-- Slide 12 -->

---

## Conversion Operator Anatomy

| Part | In `operator double() const` |
|---|---|
| Keyword | `operator` |
| Target type | `double` |
| Return type | None written: the target type is the return type |
| Parameters | None: the object being converted is the only input |
| `const` | Converting does not change the object |
| Body | Returns a value of the target type |

::: notes
A conversion operator is a special operator function, like operator() from 09.01. Writing a return type in front of it is a compile error; see the appendix.

Reading: learncpp 21.11, Overloading typecasts.
:::

<!-- Slide 13 -->

---

## Conversion Operator Anatomy

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
~~~cpp
class Temperature {
private:
    double celsius;

public:
    Temperature(double value = 0.0) { celsius = value; }

    // Converts a Temperature to its Celsius value
    operator double() const { return celsius; }
};

int main() {
    Temperature today(21.5);

    double reading = today;          // initialization
    double warmer = today + 1.5;     // arithmetic

    cout << reading << " " << warmer << endl;
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::: notes
Output: 21.5 23

Temperature has no operator+, so today + 1.5 converts today to double and adds two doubles.

Full program: cpp/temperature_conversion.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 14 -->

## Is Zero Degrees False?

~~~cpp
Temperature freezing(0.0);

if (freezing) {
    cout << "warm" << endl;
} else {
    cout << "cold" << endl;
}
~~~

. . .

Output: `cold`

::: notes
Temperature has no operator bool. Ask first whether this compiles at all, then what it prints.

Full program: cpp/zero_degrees.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 15 -->

---

## One Conversion Leads to Another

| Step | Conversion | Written by |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Temperature` to `double` | You: `operator double()` |
| 2 | `double` to `bool` | The compiler: `0.0` is `false` |

- The compiler may add one user-defined conversion to a chain of standard conversions.

::: notes
The same chain explains int whole = today; dropping the fraction: Temperature to double, then double to int. The compiler never chains two user-defined conversions.
:::

<!-- Slide 16 -->

---

## Conversion or Getter?

| Ask | Yes | No |
|---|---|---|
| Does the object stand for exactly one number? | Conversion operator | Named getter |
| Would every reader agree which number? | Conversion operator | Named getter |

- `double reading = today;` Celsius or Fahrenheit? The line does not say.
- `today.getCelsius()` says it.

::: notes
The decision is about the reader of the calling code. Topic 4 returns to this with a conversion that names its unit in the type.
:::

<!-- Slide 17 -->

---

## Summary

- `operator T() const` teaches a class to become a `T`.
- Write one only when the result has a single obvious meaning; otherwise use a named getter.

::: notes

:::
